title: Machine Learning Foundations
summary: A practical introduction to machine learning: kinds of learning, preparing data and features, training and testing, common algorithms explained simply, a first scikit-learn project, and responsible, fair use.
audience: Learners with basic Python who want to understand and start using machine learning

body.p: Machine learning (ML) lets computers learn patterns from examples instead of following rules written by hand. Show a model thousands of labelled photos of healthy and diseased cassava leaves, and it learns to label new photos. ML powers spam filters, credit scoring, crop-disease apps, translation, recommendations and chatbots.

list: Supervised learning: examples come with answers (labels). Predicting a number, such as a house price, is regression; predicting a category, such as spam or not spam, is classification.
Unsupervised learning: no labels; the model finds structure, such as groups of similar customers (clustering).
Reinforcement learning: an agent learns by trial and error from rewards, as in game playing and robotics.

body.h: When ML is (and is not) a good idea

list: Good: the pattern is too complex for simple rules, plenty of relevant data exists, and occasional mistakes are acceptable or can be checked.
Poor: a simple rule works, data is scarce or biased, or every decision must be fully explainable and error-free.

body.tip: Always ask what decision the model will support and what happens when it is wrong. That shapes everything else.

body.p: Models are only as good as their data. Each example is described by features (inputs) and, in supervised learning, a label (the answer). For predicting loan repayment, features might include income, existing debts and repayment history; the label is whether the loan was repaid.

list: Collect data that represents the people and situations the model will meet; data only from cities will mislead a model used in rural areas.
Clean it: fix errors, handle missing values and remove duplicates.
Convert categories (such as province) into numbers, for example with one-hot encoding.
Scale numerical features so large-valued ones do not dominate.
Engineer useful features, such as "days since last payment".

body.p: Leakage happens when a feature secretly contains the answer, such as a "debt written off" column when predicting default. The model then looks brilliant in testing and fails in real use. Only use information that would be available at the moment the prediction is made.

body.tip: Spend time looking at the raw data and charts before modelling; most surprises are data problems, not algorithm problems.

body.p: A model must be judged on data it has never seen. Split the data: for example 70% (700 of 1000 examples) for training and 30% for testing. Often a validation set or cross-validation is also used to choose settings, keeping the test set for one final check.

list: Underfitting: the model is too simple and does badly even on training data.
Overfitting: the model memorises training examples, including noise, and does much worse on new data.
Signs of overfitting: very high training accuracy but much lower test accuracy.
Fixes: more data, simpler models, regularisation or limiting model depth.

body.p: Accuracy can mislead when one class is rare. Suppose a fraud model checks 1000 transactions: it catches 40 frauds (true positives), raises 10 false alarms, misses 20 frauds and correctly clears 930. Accuracy is (40 + 930) / 1000 = 97%, yet a model that never flags fraud would score 95%. Precision is 40 / 50 = 80% (flags that are real) and recall is 40 / 60, about 66.7% (frauds caught).

body.tip: Choose the metric that matches the cost of mistakes: missed disease cases (recall) usually matter more than false alarms.

body.p: You do not need advanced maths to understand the main ideas behind popular algorithms.

list: Linear regression: draws the best straight line through the data to predict a number.
Logistic regression: turns a weighted sum of features into a probability for a yes/no outcome.
Decision trees: ask a series of yes/no questions ("Is income above R10 000?") to reach a prediction; easy to explain.
Random forests and gradient boosting: combine many trees for strong accuracy on tabular data.
k-nearest neighbours: predicts from the most similar past examples. With features (30, 20) and (27, 26), the Manhattan distance is |30 - 27| + |20 - 26| = 9.
k-means clustering: groups examples around k centres.
Neural networks: layers of simple units that learn complex patterns in images, sound and text; the basis of deep learning and large language models.

body.p: Start simple. A simple, explainable baseline often performs nearly as well as a complex model and shows whether complexity is worth it.

body.tip: Try a simple model first and write down its score; every later model must beat that number to earn its complexity.

body.p: Python's scikit-learn library makes the whole workflow short. The classic iris dataset has 150 flowers, each with four measurements (sepal and petal length and width) and one of three species.

body.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(len(X_train), len(X_test))
print(round(accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)), 3))
print(model.predict([[5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2]])[0])

body.p: Running this prints 105 45 (training and test sizes), then 1.0 (accuracy on the 45 test flowers) and 0 (the predicted class for a new flower, species 0, Iris setosa). These outputs were produced by running the code. A perfect score is possible here because iris is a small, clean, easy dataset; real-world problems are messier, so expect lower scores and investigate the errors.

list: random_state fixes the random split so results can be reproduced.
max_depth=3 limits the tree to reduce overfitting.
fit learns from training data; predict applies the model to new data.
Next steps: try other models, use cross-validation and look at the confusion matrix.

body.tip: Run the code in a free online notebook environment, then change one setting at a time and watch what happens.

body.p: ML decisions can affect people's loans, jobs, health and freedom, so they must be fair, explainable and monitored.

Models learn patterns from history, including past discrimination. Compare results across groups: if a hiring model shortlists 60% of one group but only 45% of another, the ratio is 0.45 / 0.6 = 0.75, below the four-fifths (0.8) guideline often used to flag possible unfair impact. Removing the sensitive attribute is not enough, because other features (such as postcode) can act as proxies.

list: Explain predictions where people are affected, and offer a way to appeal to a human.
Protect personal data under laws such as POPIA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act and GDPR.
Document the model: purpose, data, performance across groups and known limits.
Monitor after deployment: data changes over time (drift), so performance can quietly fall.
Keep humans in the loop for high-stakes decisions.

body.tip: Before building, ask who could be harmed if the model is wrong, and design checks for them first.
